title: Entity
description: Identify one modeled occurrence, distinguish identity from descriptive labels, and preserve occurrence grain when mapping entity concepts into SQL.
notes:
## An entity is one identifiable occurrence

In entity-relationship modeling, an entity is a distinguishable object or concept about which the system records information. A particular student, a particular department, or a particular course offering can be an entity. The important idea is one identifiable occurrence in the modeled domain. Student as a category is different from the particular student represented by institutional number S17.

The model follows the questions the system must answer. A campus directory may need to identify people and departments. A scheduling system may also need individual room bookings and course offerings. The same real-world setting can support different useful models because the required facts and identities differ. Do not declare an entity solely because a noun appears in a requirement sentence; determine what needs its own identity and lifecycle.

## Descriptive similarity does not establish identity

Two students can share the name Asha Rao while being distinct people. A student can change a name while remaining the same person. A reliable identifying policy therefore distinguishes occurrences independently of incidental similarities in their descriptive attributes. A required institutional number or internal identity can support that distinction under the documented scope and validity rules.

The database's identifier is a representation of the intended entity identity. It still needs a policy connecting records to real-world occurrences. Two different internal numbers do not prove the records concern different people if a duplicate was entered by mistake. Conversely, one shared name does not prove the records should be merged. Entity resolution and factual verification need appropriate domain evidence beyond a convenient displayed label.

## Entities need not be physical objects

A semester, a course offering, or a reservation can be modeled as an entity even though it is not a tangible object you can hold. The relevant question is whether it is an identifiable concept whose information and relationships the system must track. A particular offering can have a term, a section, an instructor, and enrollment relationships that persist through its lifecycle.

A vague concept still needs a precise modeled meaning. Does Course describe a catalogue subject or one scheduled offering of that subject? Does Examination describe a scheduled assessment or an individual student's attempt? These distinctions affect identity, attributes, and relationships. Explicitly stating the occurrence being modeled prevents one entity name from silently referring to several different grains of fact.

## Entity type and current occurrences differ

An entity type describes common properties and identifying rules for occurrences. An entity set is the collection of such occurrences at the relevant modeled state. Student can have no current recorded occurrences while its definition remains meaningful. Adding a new student changes that population without redefining every property of the type.

Terminology varies between introductory diagrams, where a named rectangle often stands for the type or set being discussed. Keep the intended meaning clear: Asha with identifier S17 is an occurrence; Student describes the category and its common roles. A model should not confuse one example person with the entire set or assume the absence of current examples erases the category's definition.

## Attributes describe the occurrence

Attributes record properties such as a student's name, birth date, or institutional number. The domain of each attribute describes permitted values, while the actual entity occurrence has particular values or permitted absences. A required identifying attribute and an optional descriptive attribute serve different purposes. Missing optional information does not necessarily mean the entity itself lacks an identity.

Do not turn every property into a separate entity without a reason. A simple scalar label may be adequately represented as an attribute. A maintained Programme catalogue with its own identity, name, rules, and relationships can deserve its own entity type. The decision follows reuse, meaning, relationships, and lifecycle rather than the visual width of a table or the number of characters in a label.

## Relationships connect identified occurrences

An entity participates in relationships with other occurrences. A student enrolls in a particular course offering, and an instructor teaches a particular section. The relationship connects the relevant identities, not just their descriptive names. Repeated names in two entity sets therefore do not establish a relationship by themselves.

One student can participate in several enrollment occurrences without becoming several students. A query joining the student to every enrollment may repeat the student's name across result rows. That repeated display is consistent with a relationship-grain report. Removing it automatically with DISTINCT can conceal legitimate separate participation. State whether a result describes entities, relationships, or another derived population.

## Some relationships become modeled occurrences

An enrollment can have its own grade, status, dates, and attempt identity. Depending on the chosen notation and requirements, designers can represent it as a relationship with attributes or an associative entity. Having a descriptive attribute alone does not logically force one universal choice. What matters is representing the required participants and distinguishing the intended occurrences consistently.

If one student can attempt the same course twice, the model must identify those attempts separately. A student-course pair may be insufficient, and an appropriate attempt attribute or separate occurrence identifier can be needed. The two enrollments concern one student entity but different participation occurrences. This is a useful example of why entity identity and report grain must be considered together.

## A relational mapping is a representation choice

A simple strong entity type commonly maps to a relation whose tuples represent its occurrences. Student can map to a table containing student_id and student_name. This is a useful introductory correspondence, but an entity is not defined as exactly one row across every possible schema. Normalized properties, relationships, inheritance mappings, or history can require several related relations.

Likewise, a query result row does not automatically represent a new entity. An aggregate can describe the number of enrollments, and a joined row can describe a combination of existing occurrences. Read the source model and selected result meaning before interpreting every row as a separate real-world object. The mapping should preserve identities rather than equating a physical representation with the conceptual definition.

## Query identities explicitly

A lookup for student_id seventeen should use the declared identifying value, not select whichever Asha appears first. Names can repeat and result positions can change. Include identifiers in diagnostic output when several occurrences may share descriptions. Request an explicit order when the consumer needs deterministic presentation, using a suitable identifying tie-breaker.

```sql
SELECT student_id, student_name
FROM students
WHERE student_id = 17;
```

The lookup can return no row if the recorded occurrence is absent. It does not establish the person's real-world existence or grant access to their information. The application's authorization and data-validation boundaries remain separate from the entity concept and from the correctness of a small SQL fixture.

## Preserve entities with no current participation

A student can exist in the recorded population without current enrollments if the model permits that state. An inner join to Enrollment would omit that student. A preserving join can keep the student with a zero related count when the report asks for all students. Count a nonmissing child identity rather than every preserved output row to avoid inventing one enrollment for the unmatched student.

Fixtures should include repeated names, one student with several enrollments, and one student with none. These cases reveal whether the query preserves the intended occurrences and counts the correct relationship facts. A fixture with one student and one enrollment cannot expose many identity and population mistakes because several different interpretations happen to produce the same visible row.

## Review the model through concrete occurrences

Describe several examples and counterexamples before finalizing an entity definition. Ask which occurrence each identifier denotes, which properties can change without changing identity, and whether repeated participation creates a new entity or a related fact. Also identify optional information and any required relationships so the model's legal states remain explicit.

An entity model is useful when it makes occurrences, identities, properties, and participation understandable. SQL exercises can demonstrate a selected relational mapping on synthetic data, but they do not prove every mapping choice or external identity assertion. Keep that scope clear while preserving the central distinction: one modeled occurrence is different from its category, its descriptions, and the several result rows through which its relationships may be displayed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines an entity in the ER model?
options: A table stored in a relational database
A distinctly identifiable real-world object or concept about which data is captured
A named collection of similar objects
A rule that restricts the values an attribute may take
questions.explanation: An entity is a single, distinguishable real-world object or concept — the basic unit the ER model captures data about.

questions.question_text: In the college database, which of these is an entity (a single occurrence), not a category?
options: Student
Course
Aditi Sharma, Roll No. 21CS045
Department
questions.explanation: A named, specific individual is one occurrence — an entity — while 'Student' or 'Department' names the whole category (entity set).

questions.question_text: Must an entity always represent a tangible, physical object?
options: Yes, only physical objects qualify as entities
No, intangible concepts like a course offering or a semester can also be entities
Only if it has a primary key
Only in weak entity sets
questions.explanation: Entities can be abstract/intangible (a course, a job title) as long as they are individually identifiable.

questions.question_text: Two students are both named 'Rahul Kumar' but have different roll numbers. Are they the same entity?
options: Yes, because the name is identical
No, they are distinct entities because they are different real-world occurrences with different identifying data
It depends on which department they belong to
They merge into a single entity automatically
questions.explanation: Entities are distinguished by their identifying data (like roll number), not by name similarity.

questions.question_text: What minimally must be true for something to qualify as an entity?
options: It must be stored in more than one table
The model treats it as a distinguishable occurrence about which relevant properties or relationships are recorded
It must participate in a relationship
It must have a multi-valued attribute
questions.explanation: Entity modeling follows identifiable occurrences and required facts; a fixed minimum count of descriptive attributes is not a universal definition.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes an entity from an entity set?
options: An entity set is a single instance; an entity is the whole collection
There is no difference; the terms are fully interchangeable
An entity is a single instance; an entity set is the collection of all entities of that type
An entity set only applies to weak entities
questions.explanation: This is the core entity vs. entity-set distinction: instance vs. collection of instances.

questions.question_text: Why might a single 'Enrollment' occurrence (Student X in Course Y, Semester Z, with a grade) be treated as an entity rather than a plain relationship?
options: Because relationships can never have attributes
Its identity, participants, attributes and lifecycle may make an associative-entity representation useful under the chosen model
Because enrollments never involve two entity sets
Because SQL cannot store relationships
questions.explanation: Relationships can also have attributes; descriptive data alone does not force a universal entity-versus-relationship choice.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to call something an entity?
options: It is a real-world occurrence
It is distinguishable from other occurrences of the same kind
It has describable properties
It always corresponds to exactly one row across all possible database schemas
questions.explanation: How an entity maps to rows/tables is a schema-design outcome, not part of what defines it conceptually as an entity.

questions.question_text: Two students share a name but have different justified identities. What follows?
options: They must be merged
They can remain distinct entity occurrences
The name becomes a key automatically
One must be removed
questions.explanation: Descriptions do not determine identity by themselves.

questions.question_text: Does an entity need to be tangible?
options: Yes; only physical objects qualify
Only if it has no attributes
No; a particular offering or reservation can be modeled as an entity
Only if stored in one row
questions.explanation: Identifiable domain concepts can be modeled.

questions.question_text: Why distinguish a course catalogue entry from a course offering?
options: Their names must always differ
Only one can have attributes
They represent different grains with different occurrence identities
They must use different database engines
questions.explanation: The model must specify what each occurrence means.

questions.question_text: Does a changed student name necessarily create a new student entity?
options: Yes; every new string means a new person
Only if the name is shorter
Only if no enrollments exist
No; identity can persist through descriptive changes
questions.explanation: Mutable descriptions can belong to the same occurrence.

questions.question_text: What does repeated student output after an enrollment join often mean?
options: Several relationship facts concern the same student
Several new student entities were created
All repeated rows are invalid
The student key vanished
questions.explanation: A relationship-grain result can repeat one participant identity.

questions.question_text: Can a relationship have descriptive attributes without necessarily becoming an entity in every notation?
options: No; every attribute forces a new entity
Yes; the chosen representation depends on the modeling requirements
Only if names are numeric
Only if there are no keys
questions.explanation: The model should preserve meaning rather than apply a misleading automatic rule.

questions.question_text: Why can two identical descriptive event records need separate occurrence identities?
options: All descriptions must be globally unique
Only row positions identify events
They can represent separate actual occurrences
The same person can never act twice
questions.explanation: Occurrence grain can require explicit distinction beyond descriptions.

questions.question_text: Does every query result row represent a new real-world entity?
options: Yes; SELECT always creates entities
Only if ordered
Only if it contains a number
No; it may describe an aggregate or combination
questions.explanation: Result grain follows query meaning.

questions.question_text: What does a simple Student-to-table mapping demonstrate?
options: One selected relational representation of modeled occurrences
A universal one-row-per-entity law for all schemas
Production identity verification
All inheritance mappings
questions.explanation: Conceptual identity and physical representation are not identical.

questions.question_text: How can a report keep students with no enrollment?
options: Use only an inner join
Start from students and preserve unmatched participants
Delete student ids from the projection
Count programme values instead
questions.explanation: The query population must match all intended student occurrences.

questions.question_text: Why count a child identity after a preserving enrollment join?
options: COUNT(*) always ignores NULL rows
Student names are always unique
The unmatched preserved row is not an actual enrollment
The count determines degree
questions.explanation: A nonmissing child identity counts real matched facts.

questions.question_text: What must a conceptual entity review make explicit?
options: Only the shortest table name
Only a physical file location
Only the number of screen rows
Occurrence meaning, identity and relevant participation
questions.explanation: These decisions define what the model is describing.

coding_problems.title: Select one student occurrence by identity
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and student_name for student_id 17. Do not match by name or screen position.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
constraints: Identifiers represent distinct recorded students; names can repeat.
edge_cases: The desired identity can be absent.
Another student can have the same name.
hints: Select the identity alongside the description.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, student_name FROM students WHERE student_id = 17;
coding_problems.explanation: The lookup follows the recorded occurrence identity without assuming unique names. This is a SQL mapping demonstration, not external identity verification.

coding_problems.title: Preserve student occurrences with zero participation
coding_problems.task: Return every student_id and enrollment_count. Include students with no enrollment as zero and count each supplied enrollment occurrence separately.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (enrollment_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_id INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Asha'),(3,'Mira'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,1),(2,1),(3,2);
constraints: Every supplied enrollment references a supplied student; native FK enforcement is not part of these temporary mirrors.
edge_cases: A student can have zero or several relationships.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT s.student_id, COUNT(e.enrollment_id) AS enrollment_count FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id ORDER BY s.student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The report returns one row per student occurrence while counting related enrollment facts at their separate grain.
